<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="BRPXQZME" />{{running header|{{smaller|{{asc|ODE 1.}}}}|{{asc|THE MAJOR ODES OF THE KINGDOM.}}|397}}{{rule}}</noinclude>That her childlessness might be taken away.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
She then trod on a toe-print made by God, and was moved<ref>The 'toe-print made by God' has occasioned much speculation of the critics. We may simply draw the conclusion that the poet meant to have his readers believe with him that the conception of his hero was supernatural. We saw in [[Sacred Books of the East/Volume 3/The Shih/Odes of the Temple and the Altar/The Sacrificial Odes of Shang/Ode 3|the third of the Sacrificial Odes of Shang]] that there was also a legend assigning a præternatural birth to the father of the [[Portal:Shang dynasty|House of Shang]].</ref>,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
In the large place where she rested.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
She became pregnant; she dwelt retired;{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
She gave birth to, and nourished (a son),{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Who was {{tooltip|Hâu-''k''î|Hòujì}}.

When she had fulfilled her months,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Her firstborn son (came forth) like a lamb.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
There was no bursting, nor rending,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
No injury, no hurt;{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Showing how wonderful he would be.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Did not God give her the comfort?{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}w
Had he not accepted her pure offering and sacrifice,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
So that thus easily she brought forth her son?

He was placed in a narrow lane,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
But the sheep and oxen protected him with loving care<ref name="p397_2">It does not appear from the ode who exposed the infant to these various perils; nor did Chinese tradition ever fashion any story on the subject. [[Mao Shi Zhuan|Mâo]] makes the exposure to have been made by [[w:Jiang Yuan|''K''iang Yüan]]'s husband, dissatisfied with what had taken place; [[Author:Zheng Xuan|''K''ăng]], by the mother herself, to show the more the wonderful character of her child. Readers will compare the accounts with the Roman legends about [[w:Romulus and Remus|Romulus and Remus]], their mother and her father; but the two legends differ according to the different characters of the Chinese and Roman peoples.</ref>.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
He was placed in a wide forest,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Where he was met with by the wood-cutters.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
He was placed on the cold ice,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
And a bird screened and supported him with its wings.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
When the bird went away,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Hâu-''k''î began to wail.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
His cry was long and loud,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
So that his voice filled the whole way<ref name="p397_2" />.
